newsitem.title: USA: Perry orders wide sexual harassment review.
newsitem.headline: Perry orders wide sexual harassment review.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Perry said Wednesday he had ordered all branches of the military to hammer home the message of "zero tolerance" for harassment of women in uniform.

With the Army checking sexual harassment complaints from female trainees at bases across the country since it disclosed a scandal at a training facility in Maryland last week, Perry told reporters he had asked the military services "to make sure there is not some problem there that could cause the sort of issue ... that we saw in the Army."

In response the Air Force, Army and Navy, which includes the Marines, are looking into how they communicate the Pentagon's policy of "zero tolerance" for sexual harassment, Perry said after a speech in Arlington, Virginia, to the Electronic Industries Association.

A Pentagon spokeswoman said Deputy Defence Secretary John White had asked the civilian secretaries of the services to report to him "how each service communicates the department's zero tolerance policy to all levels of command."

Perry declined comment on the misconduct cases disclosed by the Army but said sexual harassment was not only wrong ethically and morally but inimical to military discipline and "proper respect in the chain of command."
"For all of these reasons, therefore, we have zero tolerance for sexual harassment," he said.
The Army disclosed last week that a captain and two others who trained recruits faced charges including rape of female trainees at the Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.
In Kansas City, Missouri, a drill sergeant was discharged and sentenced to prison Wednesday after admitting to having sex with three female recruits.

A military judge at the Fort Leonard Wood Army base in Missouri handed a bad-conduct discharge to Staff Sgt. Loren Taylor, who was also sentenced to five months in confinemnt facility and was demoted in rank after he pleaded guilty to seven charges of misconduct. In exchange, prosecutors agreed to drop charges of obstruction of justice and perjury.
The Army said the latest charges resulted from ongoing investigations and were not related to the scandal in Maryland.
Army regulations forbid all sexual relationships between commanders and subordinates.

Pentagon officials feared the scandal would give the U.S. military another black eye after a string of harassment cases that began with the 1991 "Tailhook" scandal, in which male Navy and Marine pilots fondled women at a Las Vegas hotel.
